claims.claim: The same reviewer says that layered unreliability is not done in an intrusive, postmodern way and was subliminal enough that he missed it on a first reading.
claims.source: Vacuous Wastrel blog, review of The Golden Fool
claims.quote: It’s not done in an intrusive, postmodern way
claims.page: review of 'The Golden Fool, by Robin Hobb', final discussion paragraph

claims.claim: The same reviewer describes Hobb's language as carrying a slightly heavy and old-fashioned tone common to the genre, while still delivering memorable lines.
claims.source: Vacuous Wastrel blog, review of Fool's Quest
claims.quote: slightly heavy and old-fashioned tone common to the genre
claims.page: review of Fool's Quest, Overall section

claims.claim: The same reviewer dissents from the general praise of Hobb's prose, calling it unremarkable and saying the flashes of beautiful imagery are balanced by her willingness to describe the horrific and the ugly.
claims.source: Vacuous Wastrel blog, review of a later Elderlings novel
claims.quote: As is usually the case with Hobb, her prose is unremarkable

claims.claim: Novelist M Harold Page states a rule he derives from Fool's Assassin: Hobb delivers description only when it is part of a conflict, giving the fashionable trousers being argued over as his example.
claims.source: M Harold Page, Black Gate, 9 February 2016
claims.quote: She only delivers description when it’s part of a conflict

claims.claim: Page states a second rule: Hobb serves up characterisation at the moment it bears on a choice or tactic, illustrating with a stable hand who might teach the narrator to ride.
claims.source: M Harold Page, Black Gate, 9 February 2016
claims.quote: Hobb always serves up characterisation when it is immediately significant

claims.claim: Page identifies an unremitting rhythm of the word but at every level of Fool's Assassin, so that nothing in the book arrives without a qualification.
claims.source: M Harold Page, Black Gate, 9 February 2016
claims.quote: an unremitting rhythm of buts at all levels
claims.page: section 'Making Lyrical Fantasy Interesting', first bullet

claims.claim: Page says the qualifications nest inside one another at several scales, calling Hobb's buts fractal.
claims.source: M Harold Page, Black Gate, 9 February 2016
claims.page: section 'Making Lyrical Fantasy Interesting', first bullet

claims.claim: Page states the braiding rule he finds in Fool's Assassin: a death arising from the thriller plot carries domestic and child-rearing implications, and a death in the domestic plot sets off the thriller.
claims.source: M Harold Page, Black Gate, 9 February 2016
claims.quote: a death resulting from the Thriller has domestic and child-rearing implications
claims.page: section 'First Person Slow Burn Thriller', bullet on braiding

claims.claim: Page says Hobb links the domestic and political plots practically and not only thematically, the same duty manifesting in both.
claims.source: M Harold Page, Black Gate, 9 February 2016
claims.quote: the same duty manifests both domestically and politically

claims.claim: Page describes Hobb's substitute for a viewpoint shift in a first-person thriller: information is dropped after the fact but in a way that points forward.
claims.source: M Harold Page, Black Gate, 9 February 2016
claims.quote: She drops information on us after-the-fact but in ways that point forward

claims.claim: Page notes that the retrospective narrator's editorialising is confined to bookending episodes so that it does not break the flow of the narrative.
claims.source: M Harold Page, Black Gate, 9 February 2016
claims.quote: only to bookend episodes, and does not break the flow

verdicts.trueWording: It’s not done in an intrusive, postmodern way – it’s so subliminal I don’t think I really picked up on it the first time I read it – but every level of the narration is imperfect.
verdicts.note: Found in the raw tag-archive page (curl, browser UA), inside 'The Golden Fool, by Robin Hobb' (4 Feb 2013), in the final discussion paragraph ('Finally: on this re-read, I continue to be struck by the ambiguity of the narration...') immediately before the Adrenaline/Emotion ratings, exactly as the claim's page-locator says. Quote is word-for-word. Layered unreliability limb supported ('the Fitz of the past can't be trusted... should we really trust Fitz-the-narrator?', 'every level of the narration is imperfect'); missed-on-first-reading limb supported verbatim. Only unsupported detail is the reviewer's gender ('he'), which the page does not state — too trivial to downgrade.

verdicts.trueWording: while the language does have that slightly heavy and old-fashioned tone common to the genre, that doesn’t prevent it from delivering fantastic lines, whether melancholy ruminations on life or just witty deadpan remarks
verdicts.note: Same raw page, inside the 'Fool's Quest, by Robin Hobb' review, in the 'Overall: 7/7. BRILLIANT' paragraph — the exact section the claim names. Quote word-for-word. 'Memorable lines' is the claim's paraphrase of 'fantastic lines, whether melancholy ruminations on life or just witty deadpan remarks', which the page supports directly.

verdicts.trueWording: Beauty: 3/5. As is usually the case with Hobb, her prose is unremarkable, and the flashes of beautiful imagery are balanced by her willingness to describe the horrific and the ugly.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that the reviewer 'dissents from the general praise of Hobb's prose' — the page never mentions any general or received praise of her prose, so no dissent is stated or implied; 'as is usually the case with Hobb' means 'across her books', not 'contrary to what others say'
verdicts.note: Quote is verbatim and the rest of the claim is verbatim too: the Beauty 3/5 line is in the 'Dragon Keeper, by Robin Hobb' review (13 Apr 2014), a later Elderlings novel as the claim says (the page itself calls it 'essentially the tenth novel of the combined Realm of Elderlings cycle'). The dissent framing is the claim-writer's, not the page's; the nearest thing on the page runs the other way — in the Fool's Quest review he notes 'Literary afficionados will complain that it is not a prose poem'. Graded PARTIAL on that limb alone.

verdicts.trueWording: She only delivers description when it’s part of a conflict: Here are the fashionable trousers we’re arguing about.
verdicts.note: Raw Black Gate article fetched with a browser UA (HTTP 200, 158 KB). Quote word-for-word in the 'Making Lyrical Fantasy Interesting' section, and the trousers example is the sentence's own illustration. 'Novelist M Harold Page' is supported by the page's own bio line ('the sword-wielding author of works of lyrical and poetic magical realism... such as Swords vs Tanks'), and the piece is explicitly a dissection of Fool's Assassin.

verdicts.trueWording: Hobb always serves up characterisation when it is immediately significant to choices or tactics adopted by the main characters. Here’s a quirky stable hand, will he teach me to ride?
verdicts.note: Quote word-for-word in the same 'Making Lyrical Fantasy Interesting' section; the choice-or-tactic limb and the stable-hand illustration are both on the page verbatim. One ordering nuance worth recording: on the page this characterisation rule is stated BEFORE the description rule of index 378, so 'a second rule' is the claim-list's numbering, not the article's.

verdicts.trueWording: Hobb uses an unremitting rhythm of buts at all levels of the story (note the single “t”). Nothing arrives without a “but”.
verdicts.note: Quote word-for-word as the first bullet under 'First, the writing is just plain good' inside the 'Making Lyrical Fantasy Interesting' section — the locator is right. 'At every level of Fool's Assassin' = 'at all levels of the story'; 'nothing arrives without a qualification' = 'Nothing arrives without a “but”'. Both limbs supported.

Quote word-for-word, closing the same first bullet. The nesting-at-several-scales limb is carried by the bullet's own chained example ('Here’s a character who needs rescuing, but she’s not very nice, but she’s vulnerable but she’s…') plus 'at all levels of the story'; 'fractal' is the author's own word for that self-similarity, so the gloss is the page's sense, not an addition.

verdicts.trueWording: She braids the plots together. For example, a death resulting from the Thriller has domestic and child-rearing implications. A death in the Period Drama sets off developments in the Thriller.
verdicts.note: Quote word-for-word in the 'First Person Slow Burn Thriller' section, in the braiding bullet the claim names. The reciprocal limb is on the page as the very next sentence; the claim's 'domestic plot' for the article's 'Period Drama' is the article's own equation (the Period Drama is where the characters are 'caught up in domestic and relationship plot').

verdicts.trueWording: She uses themes like duty, friendship, love and self-determination to link both plots, not just thematically but also practically: the same duty manifests both domestically and politically.
verdicts.note: Quote word-for-word in the 'First Person Slow Burn Thriller' section. Both limbs — 'practically and not only thematically' and 'the same duty manifesting in both' — are in that one sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: She drops information on us after-the-fact but in ways that point forward.
verdicts.note: Quote word-for-word in the 'First Person Slow Burn Thriller' section. The substitute-for-a-viewpoint-shift limb is supported by the immediate context: the section opens by saying the thriller cross-cut 'You can’t do this if you are writing in first person!', and the preceding paragraph says 'We don’t need a point-of-view shift to tell us that the ninjas have arrived.'

verdicts.trueWording: she’s very careful to do this only to bookend episodes, and does not break the flow of the narrative.
verdicts.note: Quote word-for-word in the 'First Person Slow Burn Thriller' section. The retrospective-narrator limb is supported by the same bullet: 'She “cheats” by having the narrator editorialise. Most of it is written in First Person Old Guy, so it fits the voice to have just the occasional rueful, “If only I’d known…”'.
